points: * Applebee writing patte unspecified w * The operative ontology of writing instruction is artifact-driven: writing means producing a known-form essay, learning to write means accumulating practice at that production, and the cognitive activity of composing (entering uncertainty, discovering what you think through drafting) is assumed but never probed -- making it invisible to loss. * Four actors hold incompatible definitions of what writing instruction is: grades for the parent, standards coverage for the administrator, procedure for the student, and an unarticulated intention for the teacher -- producing confusion rather than shared frameworks when AI arrives. * diSessa and Cobb's ontological innovation sets a strict standard: a genuine construct must change what practitioners design, what students experience, what assessment accomplishes, and what parents attend to -- and virtually none of the current AI-writing vocabulary meets this test. * The student is the only actor who knows what actually happened in the room with the AI model -- whether they pushed back sentence by sentence, used it as a thought partner, or accepted the draft wholesale -- yet schools rely entirely on the artifact and never ask.
quotes: A parent w word here, a describe wh significant ha "Whether something was lost is a judgment requiring expertise. Whether something might have been learned from the writing assignment is the question that the usual framing -- deficit, struggle removed -- won't even let the parent ask. It's already been answered.

Writing is treated as the production of an artifact in a known form. Learning to write is treated as accumulating practice at producing the artifact. The cognitive activity of composing -- entering uncertainty, holding a thought long enough to interrogate it, discovering through writing that one did not know one thought -- is not part of the operative account, even when it appears in policy documents as a goal.

Write an essay arguing a thesis about Homer's construal of honor is not a writing assignment. It is a reading assignment in essay-shaped costume. The assignment expects students to learn about honor, not about writing.

The four actors can say neither what was lost nor what was gained through using a bot because the ontology of writing instruction is driven by artifacts, not by cognition. The procedure is the learning activity. The artifact is the proof of completion. The grade is the measure. Cognitive activity is assumed, not probed.

Leave out the student and you lose the only person who knows what actually happened in the room with the model. Only the student knows whether the bot's draft appeared and produced the relief of not having to start from blank, or whether the student read it and pushed back against it sentence by sentence, or whether the student used it as a thought partner and sifted its answers.

The institution's first task is not to draft a new AI policy. It is the work before the work: expose what each position assumes, surface where the assumptions conflict, and ask whether the operative account of writing instruction in this school is one anyone in the building can defend on inspection.
Schools cannot ask what AI is doing to writing until they can say what writing instruction is.
